description: SpacENKA, Enka Teknik Okulları bünyesinde yazılım ve mühendislik odaklı çalışan bir teknoloji takımıdır. NASA Space Apps Challenge kapsamında, uzay görevlerinde astronot sağlığını ve kritik yaşamsal verileri takip eden güvenilir, gerçek zamanlı ve çevrimdışı (offline-first) yazılım çözümleri geliştirmekteyiz.
summary: The space environment can make it difficult for astronauts to monitor their health status in real time. Building on this, we developed an application that makes it easier for astronauts to track their health status instantaneously. Thanks to this application, astronauts can monitor vital health data (heart rate, blood oxygen level, body temperature, etc.) through a single, easy-to-understand interface. The application also includes a survey that provides mental health monitoring to track mental health risks such as depression, as well as a help section for situations involving risks of self-harm. Additionally, the application can simulate different health conditions that are likely to occur in a space environment.
details:
AstroHealth is an offline desktop application written in Python using PyQt6 and PyQtGraph. It does not use a web server or a remote backend. When the program starts through main.py, it creates the PyQt application, loads the interface and logo, initializes a local SQLite database at ~/.astrohealth/astrohealth.sqlite3, creates the main dashboard window, and starts the Qt event loop. This event loop listens for user actions, timer events, and telemetry signals generated by the simulator.

The graphical interface is implemented in ui/dashboard.py. It displays the current heart rate, blood oxygen level, body temperature, radiation level, and heart-rate variability. Each metric card shows the current value, its unit, the configured normal range, and a status such as NORMAL, WARNING, or CRITICAL. The dashboard also includes real-time charts for heart rate and radiation, an anomaly incident log, scenario controls, crew age selection, a well-being check, emergency support, mission parameters, and a JSON export function.

Telemetry is generated by the TelemetrySimulator class in core/simulator.py. This class runs in a separate QThread, so the user interface remains responsive while new readings are generated. Normally, the simulator produces one synthetic telemetry sample per second. The values are generated using random distributions rather than real sensors. Heart rate is created around a normal resting value, SpO₂ and body temperature are generated within configured ranges, radiation is normally between 0.05 and 0.20 mSv/h, and HRV is generated according to the selected crew profile.

The crew profile is defined in core/crew_profile.py. The operator can select an age between 26 and 46 because all astronauts are between the ages of 26-46. The predicted maximum heart rate is calculated using the formula 220 - age. The warning heart-rate threshold is approximately 85 percent of this maximum, while the critical threshold is the maximum itself. HRV ranges also depend on age: the configured range is 55–85 ms for ages 26–35 and 40–65 ms for ages 36–46. SpO₂ is normally configured between 95 and 99 percent, while body temperature is configured between 36.5 and 37.5 degrees Celsius.

The simulator also supports several manually triggered scenarios. Hypoxia lowers SpO₂, increases heart rate, and decreases HRV. A solar particle event increases the radiation dose rate rapidly and then gradually returns it to background levels. Fever increases body temperature, raises resting heart rate, and lowers HRV. EVA exertion increases heart rate and decreases HRV before recovery. Bradycardia lowers the heart rate to a critical level, cold exposure lowers body temperature, and autonomic strain raises heart rate while reducing HRV. Scenarios have durations and groups. Scenarios in the same group replace one another, while scenarios from different groups can run simultaneously. The recovery button clears all active scenarios and returns the simulator to nominal readings.

The anomaly detection logic is located in core/anomaly_engine.py. The AnomalyEngine evaluates every telemetry sample against the selected crew profile and returns any active findings. A heart rate below 40 bpm or at or above the age-based maximum is classified as critical, while a value outside the configured range is classified as a warning. SpO₂ below 92 percent is critical, and values outside the normal range are warnings. Body temperature above 38.5 degrees Celsius is critical, and values outside the configured range are warnings. Radiation above 1.5 mSv/h is critical, radiation above 0.20 mSv/h is a warning, and HRV below ten milliseconds under its configured lower limit is critical. Each anomaly includes the affected metric, severity, message, and sometimes additional NASA-related hazard context.

The simulator sends each generated sample through a PyQt signal called sample_ready. The dashboard listens to this signal and processes every sample in its _handle_sample method. First, it verifies that the received object is a valid TelemetrySample. Then it evaluates the sample with the anomaly engine, updates the metric cards, determines the overall crew status, updates the charts, manages active incidents, and saves the reading to SQLite. The overall status is based on the most severe active anomaly: if there are no anomalies the status is NORMAL, if there is at least one warning it is WARNING, and if there is at least one critical finding it is CRITICAL.

The application maintains an incident lifecycle. When an anomaly appears for the first time, it is opened in the database. While it remains active, the same incident stays open. When the anomaly disappears or its severity changes, the previous incident is resolved with a resolution timestamp. This allows the system to record when a problem started and when it ended instead of simply storing isolated alerts.

The local backend is implemented by TelemetryDatabase in core/database.py. It uses SQLite and stores telemetry in the telemetry_logs table. Each record contains the timestamp, heart rate, SpO₂, body temperature, radiation, HRV, overall status, cumulative radiation dose, and simulation session ID. Anomalies are stored in the anomaly_incidents table with their opening time, resolution time, severity, metric, message, and optional hazard context. The database uses locking for thread safety and enables SQLite’s WAL mode to improve reliability during ongoing reads and writes.

The simulator also calculates cumulative radiation dose for each simulation session. Because radiation is measured in mSv/h, the application estimates the dose by multiplying the average radiation rate between two readings by the elapsed time and converting seconds into hours. Each simulator run receives a unique session ID, allowing the total dose to be tracked separately for each session.

When the operator selects “Export mission health log,” the application reads the telemetry and incident records from SQLite and writes them to a JSON file. The exported file includes the telemetry logs, anomaly incidents, mission parameters, reference values, hazard descriptions, research examples, and a telemetry_origin field indicating that the data is synthetic. The export operation is completely local and does not require an internet connection.

The application also includes a WHO-5 well-being check implemented in ui/wellbeing.py. The user answers five questions about their well-being during the previous two weeks. Each answer receives a value from 0 to 5, and the total is multiplied by four to produce a score from 0 to 100. If the score is below 50, the application opens a support screen recommending a private check-in with the mission medical team. The well-being answers and score are kept in memory and are not added to the telemetry database or export files.

The “I need help now” button opens an offline emergency-support dialog independently of the telemetry status. It provides instructions to alert a nearby crewmate, contact the onboard medical officer, and follow the mission’s emergency medical procedure. Opening this screen does not send a message or create a database record. The mission parameters and About sections display the NASA, CSA, NOAA, and WHO references used to provide context for the simulation, but these references do not provide live data to the application.

When the application is closed, the dashboard stops its timer, requests the simulator thread to stop, waits for the worker thread to finish, closes the SQLite connection, and then exits. The project includes automated tests for anomaly classification, age-dependent thresholds, scenario behavior, recovery, SQLite persistence, JSON export, and simulator thread signals. Overall, AstroHealth works as a local pipeline in which a background simulator generates synthetic telemetry, the anomaly engine evaluates it, the PyQt dashboard displays it, and the SQLite database stores it for later review or export.
